@graph.name: API 101
@graph.abstract: Learn what an application programming interface is and what County leaders should ask before they build or buy one.

@graph.name: Overview
@graph.marin:text: An application programming interface, or API, is a connection between two computer programs. One program sends a request, and the other sends back a response. For example, a weather sensor with an API replies with a weather report when a program sends it the right message. The message is the request. The report is the response. An API works like a contract: it states what you can ask for and what you will get back. Anyone with data can offer an API, including governments and vendors.

@graph.name: Why it matters
marin:items: A vendor's API lets County systems connect to the products you buy and share their data.
A product with no API cannot link to your other systems this way.
A steady, well-described County API lets other teams and vendors build on it with confidence.
A public API lets residents and companies use County data in their own tools.

@graph.name: Problem
@graph.marin:text: An API that is not written down comes with no guarantee for the people who use it. A change to an API can break the systems that depend on it. A product with no API gives other systems no way to connect to it.

@graph.name: Solution
@graph.marin:text: Ask for an API before you buy, and get it described in writing. Treat each County API as a service with an owner. Describe it in a shared standard such as OpenAPI, and warn users before you change or retire any part.

@graph.name: User stories
marin:items: As a buyer, I want to know if a product has an API, so we can link it to our systems.
As a department head, I want our systems to share data, so staff do not enter a record twice.
As a vendor, I want a clear guide to the County's API, so I can connect without guessing.
As a resident, I want to use County data in an app I pick, so I can find what I need fast.

marin:items.definition: A connection that lets one program ask another program for data or for an action.
A message that asks a system for data or an action. The system sends back a response.
One place where a system can be reached to get a certain kind of data or action.
A document that explains how a connection between programs works and how to use it.
An open standard for describing web APIs in a file that both people and tools can read.
A public connection that anyone can use. It may need free sign-up and may limit use.
A connection only the organization’s own staff and contractors can use.
A connection that only chosen business partners may use.
Marked as likely to change or end. Users should plan to move away from it.
A connection a software seller offers so that County systems can work with its product.

marin:items.do: Ask each vendor for its API description before you buy.
marin:items.dont: Count on vendor features that are not documented.

marin:items.do: Name an owner for every API.
marin:items.dont: Leave an API with no one in charge.

marin:items.do: Describe each API in a shared standard such as OpenAPI.
marin:items.dont: Make other teams guess how an API works.

marin:items.do: Warn users before you change or retire an API.
marin:items.dont: Change an API without telling the people who use it.

marin:items.do: Mark the unstable parts so users know they may change.
marin:items.dont: Promise stability that you cannot keep.

@graph.name: Questions to ask
marin:items: Does this product have an API, and is it described in writing?
Who owns this API, and who do we call when it breaks?
Is it private, partner-only, or public?
Where is it described, and is that description kept up to date?
How will users learn about a change before it happens?
What data does it share, and who approved that?
How do we know who is using it, and how much?
Could a new vendor learn to use it from the documentation alone?

marin:items.title: api.data.gov, a U.S. federal service that helps agencies share APIs

@graph.name: Checklist
marin:items: We know whether each product we buy has an API.
Each API has a named owner.
Each API is marked private, partner, or public.
A written description of each API exists and is current.
Users are told before an API changes or ends.
Someone can see who uses each API.
Parts that may change are labeled as unstable.

@graph.name: Mantras
marin:items: Ask the vendor before you buy.
Treat an API as a contract.
Describe it before you build it.
Tell users before you change it.
